name: Hair fibres (Toppik)

lead: Hair fibres such as Toppik make thinning hair look denser within minutes. Sprinkled over sparse areas, they cover visible scalp gaps for an instantly fuller look.

The fine fibres bind to existing hair through static electricity, thickening each strand's appearance and reducing visible scalp. It is a cover-up that lasts until the next wash and does not regrow hair. Published research includes a 2017 microscopy analysis of five brands.

paras: Users shake or spray the fibres onto dry hair over thin spots, pat them in, and often set them with a hold spray. The look lasts until washed out, so it is reapplied daily, and it is often used alongside hair-loss treatments.
A 2020 case report described anterior uveitis after a fibre from a hair-building product entered the eye of a 73-year-old man. Keep the fibres out of the eyes and avoid inhaling them.

angle.text: Users sprinkle Toppik-style fibres over thinning areas to make hair look denser within minutes. The fibres cling to existing hair and cover scalp gaps, and the fuller look lasts until washed out.

lead: Hair fibres, sold under brands such as Toppik, are cosmetic products made of fine fibres that adhere to the hair shaft by electrostatic attraction to disguise hair loss in men and women. [1]
A 2017 study used scanning electron microscopy and X-ray microanalysis to compare five brands of organic hair fibres. [1] No efficacy trials were found in the sources reviewed.

paras: No studies found of clinical outcomes. A laboratory study analysed the shape, structure and chemical composition of five brands of reconstructive hair fibres. [1] A 2020 case report described a 73-year-old man with his first episode of acute anterior uveitis, found to have a white fibre penetrating the cornea into the anterior chamber, which he identified as coming from a cosmetic hair-building product. [2]
The reported harm is a single case of ocular foreign-body injury and uveitis; the authors discussed earlier literature on small foreign fibres causing eye disease. [2]
